extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in U.S. politics, investigative reporting, and intelligence assessments
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the credibility, corroboration, and plausibility of allegations in an investigative political dossier (here, the Steele dossier). Useful for reporters, researchers, and readers judging claims about clandestine activity, kompromat, and intelligence reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent corroboration by official investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether independent investigations (e.g., the Mueller Report, Senate Intelligence Committee, U.S. intelligence agencies, special counsel) confirm the dossier's assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that 'The Mueller Report confirmed that the dossier was correct that the Kremlin was behind the appearance of the DNC emails on WikiLeaks' and that 'some of the dossier's broad threads have now been independently corroborated.' Use corroboration from authoritative, independent probes to elevate credibility of specific claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to corroborate substantive allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether investigators were able to corroborate the dossier's substantive allegations (not just peripheral details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspector General and Durham findings are cited: the IG said much of the material 'could not be corroborated', and the Durham report stated 'the FBI was not able to corroborate a single substantive allegation contained in the Steele Reports.' Lack of substantive corroboration materially weakens claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source credibility and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the dossier's sources are known, credible, and verifiable (including whether sources can be identified or have relevant access/authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes Steele and FBI practice: 'We did not ever take the information he provided at face value... independently verify the source's credibility.' Anonymous or undisclosed sources (e.g., Danchenko's sources he 'still won't reveal') reduce verifiability; assess source history, motive, and corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rumor/innuendo from direct evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether assertions are based on direct, observed evidence or on rumor, hearsay, or innuendo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Danchenko's account is described as 'his evidence really only being rumors and innuendo' and having 'never viewed' the alleged tape. Treat rumor-based claims skeptically and require stronger corroboration before accepting sensational allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and stability of witness/testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether witnesses give consistent accounts over time; changes undermine reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rtskhiladze 'changed his story between interviews' and that change was used to cast doubt. Inconsistent testimony or shifting accounts are important red flags when evaluating claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of corroboration (time/location/title vs. substantive facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether corroboration is limited to peripheral details (time, location, job titles) or extends to substantive, unique factual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Inspector General found that 'the limited information that was corroborated related to time, location, and title information, much of which was publicly available.' Corroboration of trivial details does not by itself validate the dossier's central allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility in light of known intelligence practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether allegations are plausible given documented foreign intelligence behaviors (e.g., collecting kompromat) and the broader factual record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Senate report 'found that the Russian intelligence services clearly engage in the collection of compromising information for leverage'—this context can make certain allegations plausible even if specific proof is lacking. Plausibility is useful but insufficient without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of third‑party technical or forensic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether independent technical/forensic reports support the dossier's technical or cyber-related claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an FTI Consulting report (commissioned by BuzzFeed) affirmed aspects of allegations about botnets and porn traffic. For cyber allegations, neutral forensic analysis can materially strengthen a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standards and outcomes affecting credibility (defamation/statement truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether legal findings or litigation outcomes bear on the truth or treatment of specific assertions (e.g., defamation rulings, Section 230 protections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Page defamation suit outcome (judge ruled articles 'either true or protected under Section 230') is cited. Legal rulings can confirm factual accuracy or limit remedies, and should be considered when assessing published claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and redaction limiting public verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether classification, redactions, or withheld material prevent public verification of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes 'public verification is hindered because the information is classified' and large redactions in the Senate report. A lack of public evidence due to classification should be noted as a verification constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat claims as potentially mixed true/false (granularity of assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate each allegation on its own merits; some parts of a dossier may be true while others are false or exaggerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill Priestap's quote: 'We absolutely understood that the information in the so-called dossier could be inaccurate. We also understood that some parts could be true and other parts false.' Do not treat the dossier as monolithically true or false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative rigor: attempt to prove or disprove each assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether investigators sought to independently verify, prove, or disprove every assertion rather than accepting them at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FBI investigators 'went to great lengths to try to independently verify the source's credibility and to prove or disprove every single assertion in the dossier.' Thorough verification efforts increase confidence in confirmed items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and circumstantial indicators (timing, motive, coordinating acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using timing and circumstantial facts (e.g., timing of email releases, meetings around privatizations, platform language changes) to evaluate intent or coordination claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dossier and subsequent reporting use timing (e.g., DNC leaks timed around the convention) and campaign actions (platform language changes) as evidence of coordination. Such indicators can be probative, especially when combined with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of assessment over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that factual assessments can change as new evidence emerges; claims once unverified may later be corroborated (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page observes 'Some of the dossier's broad threads have now been independently corroborated' while other elements remained uncorroborated or disputed. Update judgments with new, credible information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of source motivation, relationships, and potential bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether sources have motives, disputes, or relationships (e.g., employment disputes, political motives) that could color their information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Olga Galkina's messy dispute with Webzilla is cited as Steele's source for hacking allegations. Source disputes or personal motives can reduce reliability and should be investigated.
